specPoints.text: practical: investigate density using direct measurements of mass and volume

primer.text: Three objects, three techniques, one equation. These lessons walk the core practical: regular shapes from their dimensions, irregular shapes from displaced water, liquids from a mass difference — with the error discipline that earns the evaluation marks.

lessons.title: Regular objects: dimensions and mass
sourceHeadings: Experiment 1: measuring the density of regularly shaped objects
Equipment needed to determine the density of regularly shaped objects
lessons.opening: A regular shape surrenders its volume to a ruler or calipers. Weigh the object, measure its dimensions, rebuild the volume with the shape's formula, then divide — and repeat every reading so an average can steady the result.
keyPoints: The experiment determines the densities of regular objects from measurements of their dimensions.
The object is weighed on a digital balance, its dimensions taken with ruler, vernier calipers or micrometer, and repeats averaged.
The choice of length instrument follows the object's size — ruler for larger objects, calipers and micrometer for smaller ones.
The shape's volume formula then feeds the density equation.

low.restatement: Weigh, measure, rebuild, divide: the four-beat rhythm of every density practical. A big block surrenders to a ruler; a small one needs the finer jaws of calipers or a micrometer.
low.analogy: Tailoring: the tape (ruler) fits the coat, the fine ruler (calipers) fits the cuff — pick the instrument whose resolution matches the job.
low.examPointer: Name the repeats and the average explicitly — 'each measurement is repeated and averaged' — that sentence carries method marks.

medium.restatement: Experiment 1's discipline is instrument matching and repetition: the balance fixes the mass once, but lengths are read to the instrument's resolution, chosen by object size, and every reading is repeated so averages suppress random error. The reconstructed volume then divides the mass under the density equation.
medium.analogy: A survey crew: one instrument per scale of feature, and every measurement logged twice because single readings lie.
medium.examPointer: In write-ups, pair each instrument with its purpose — balance for mass, ruler/calipers/micrometer for dimensions — and close with the repeat-and-average sentence.

check.stem: Which instrument suits measuring a small object's dimensions most precisely?

options.text: a micrometer
options.explanation: Its 0.001 mm resolution is the finest of the three.

options.text: a 30 cm ruler
options.explanation: Its 1 mm resolution is the coarsest.

options.text: a digital balance
options.explanation: The balance measures mass, not length.

options.text: a measuring cylinder
options.explanation: That reads liquid volumes.

check.stem: What is the dependent variable in the regular-objects experiment?

options.text: the mass of the object
options.explanation: Mass answers to the changed shape or volume.

options.text: the type of shape or volume
options.explanation: That is the independent variable.

options.text: the density of water
options.explanation: Water is not part of experiment 1.

options.text: the ruler's resolution
options.explanation: Resolution is fixed by the instrument.

check.stem: Why are the dimension measurements repeated and averaged?

options.text: to reduce the random error in the length readings
options.explanation: Averaging evens out the scatter of single readings.

options.text: to fix any zero error on the balance
options.explanation: Zero errors are systematic and need re-zeroing, not averaging.

options.text: because the balance requires three readings
options.explanation: The balance reading is taken once per object.

options.text: to change the object's true volume
options.explanation: Repetition reveals the value; it never changes the object.

check.stem: Which sequence states the regular-objects method correctly?

options.text: weigh the object, measure its dimensions, average repeats, calculate density
options.explanation: Mass, dimensions, repeats, then the equation.

options.text: fill the eureka can, lower the object, read the displacement
options.explanation: That is the irregular-objects technique.

options.text: zero the balance with liquid aboard, then weigh
options.explanation: The balance is zeroed empty, never loaded with liquid.

options.text: measure the volume directly with a micrometer
options.explanation: A micrometer reads lengths, not volumes.

check.stem: After the volume is rebuilt from the dimensions, what completes the density determination?

options.text: divide the averaged mass by the volume
options.explanation: ρ = m ÷ V closes the practical.

options.text: multiply the mass by the volume
options.explanation: The equation divides.

options.text: subtract the volume from the mass
options.explanation: Subtracting unlike quantities is meaningless.

options.text: compare the mass with water's density alone
options.explanation: The division by the object's own volume is required.

check.stem: State the aim of the regular-objects experiment.
check.modelAnswer: The experiment determines the densities of regular objects from their measured dimensions and their mass.

check.stem: State which three instruments can take the dimension measurements, in decreasing size suitability.
check.modelAnswer: The 30 cm ruler serves larger objects, the vernier calipers smaller ones, and the micrometer the smallest objects.

check.stem: Explain why the digital balance reading is taken before any dimension work begins.
check.modelAnswer: The mass is a single direct reading best taken cleanly at the start, so the object is weighed first and its dimensions gathered afterwards. Sequencing the weighing first also keeps handling from transferring moisture or grease that would bias the mass.

check.stem: A student measures a cube's edge three times: 10 mm, 11 mm and 10 mm. State the averaged edge and explain the benefit of averaging.
check.modelAnswer: The averaged edge is (10 + 11 + 10) ÷ 3 ≈ 10.3 mm, and averaging steadies the random scatter of single readings so the volume — and hence the density — rests on a fairer value.

lessons.title: Irregular objects: the displacement technique
sourceHeadings: Experiment 2: measuring the density of irregularly shaped objects
Equipment needed to determine the density of irregularly shaped objects
lessons.opening: An irregular object hides its volume from any ruler. The eureka can solves that: submerged, the object pushes out its own volume of water, and the displaced water read in a measuring cylinder becomes the volume the equation needs.
keyPoints: The experiment finds the densities of irregular objects through a displacement technique.
The eureka can overflows until the water settles; the object then displaces its own volume into the measuring cylinder below the spout.
The volume of displaced water equals the volume of the object.
The object is lowered in gently — dropping splashes water and corrupts the volume reading.

low.restatement: Fill the can until it just stops overflowing, empty the cylinder, then lower the odd-shaped treasure in. Whatever spills through the spout is exactly the treasure's volume — read it, average repeats, divide the mass by it.
low.analogy: Climbing into a full bathtub: the slop over the sides is your own volume, measured where it lands.
low.examPointer: State the displacement equality explicitly — displaced volume equals object volume — and warn against splashing.

medium.restatement: Displacement converts an unmeasurable shape into a readable liquid volume: the can's spout delivers exactly the submerged object's volume into the cylinder, since displaced volume equals object volume. Gentle lowering protects the reading from splash losses, and repeats with averaging finish the discipline before the density equation divides.
medium.analogy: A slot machine paying out in water: whatever you feed it, it returns the object's volume in a readable column — unless you jolt the machine and spill extra.
medium.examPointer: In the write-up, the displaced volume step is where marks live: name the eureka can, the cylinder below the spout, and the gentle lowering.

check.stem: What does the volume of displaced water equal?

options.text: the volume of the submerged object
options.explanation: Displacement hands over the object's volume exactly.

options.text: the mass of the object
options.explanation: Mass comes from the balance.

options.text: the density of the water
options.explanation: Density is not what the spout delivers.

options.text: half the object's volume
options.explanation: The displacement is complete, not partial.

check.stem: Why must the measuring cylinder sit below the spout before the object goes in?

options.text: so none of the displaced water is lost before it is read
options.explanation: Every drop of displacement must reach the cylinder.

options.text: so the object has somewhere to land
options.explanation: The object goes into the can, not the cylinder.

options.text: so the can can be emptied first
options.explanation: Emptying the cylinder is a separate preparatory step.

options.text: so the water warms to room temperature
options.explanation: Temperature is not the concern here.

check.stem: What is the dependent variable in the irregular-objects experiment?

options.text: the volume of displaced water
options.explanation: Displacement answers to each new shape or mass.

options.text: the type of irregular shape or mass
options.explanation: That is the independent variable.

options.text: the can's overflow rate
options.explanation: Overflow is preparatory, not the measured outcome.

options.text: the density of the object
options.explanation: Density is the final calculation, not the variable read.

check.stem: Why lower the object gently rather than drop it?

options.text: dropping splashes water out, giving an incorrect volume reading
options.explanation: Splash losses corrupt the displacement.

options.text: the object might dissolve
options.explanation: Dissolving is not the cited risk.

options.text: gentle objects displace more water
options.explanation: Displacement depends on volume, not on entry speed.

options.text: the spout closes when startled
options.explanation: Nothing closes; physics is not sentimental.

check.stem: Which extra step does the irregular-object method need that the regular-object method does not?

options.text: collecting displaced water from a eureka can
options.explanation: Displacement replaces the geometry step.

options.text: weighing the object on a balance
options.explanation: Both methods weigh the object.

options.text: repeating readings and averaging
options.explanation: Both methods repeat and average.

options.text: using the density equation
options.explanation: Both methods end in the same equation.

check.stem: State the aim of the irregular-objects experiment.
check.modelAnswer: The experiment finds the densities of irregular objects through a displacement technique.

check.stem: State what must be done with the measuring cylinder just before lowering the object in.
check.modelAnswer: An empty measuring cylinder is placed below the spout, and the cylinder is emptied of any earlier overflow before the object enters.

check.stem: Explain why the eureka can is filled until water overflows and then allowed to settle before the object is added.
check.modelAnswer: Filling to overflowing guarantees the can is full to the spout's lip, so any later displacement escapes only through the spout. Allowing it to settle means the pre-experiment drips have finished; without that, stray drips would join the object's true displacement and inflate the reading.

check.stem: An irregular object of mass 240 g displaces 30 cm³ of water. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
check.modelAnswer: Density = 240 ÷ 30 = 8 g/cm³, since the displaced volume equals the object's volume.

lessons.title: Liquids and the evaluation discipline
sourceHeadings: Experiment 3: measuring the density of liquids
Equipment needed to determine the density of liquid
lessons.opening: A liquid's volume reads directly off the cylinder, but its mass needs subtraction: weigh the empty cylinder, add liquid, weigh again, and the difference is the liquid's mass. Zeroing the balance and steady handling carry the evaluation marks.
keyPoints: The liquid experiment finds the liquid's mass by subtracting the empty cylinder's mass from the filled reading.
The volume is read from the cylinder's scale when the liquid is added.
The balance is zeroed with the empty cylinder aboard before liquid is added — a systematic-error guard.
Repeats and averages limit random error, and glassware plus electrical balance demand careful handling.

low.restatement: Weigh the empty cylinder, pour to a chosen volume, weigh again; the difference is purely the liquid. Set the balance to zero first or the cylinder's own mass sneaks into every reading.
low.analogy: Packing a suitcase on a scale: weigh the case, pack, weigh again — the contents' weight is the difference, never the total.
low.examPointer: For evaluation marks, name the zeroing as a systematic-error fix and the repeats as a random-error fix — the two error families are examined separately.

medium.restatement: Experiment 3's mass is a difference: filled-cylinder reading minus empty-cylinder reading, with the balance zeroed aboard the empty cylinder so the liquid's mass alone survives. Volume comes from the cylinder's scale; repeats average the random scatter of pouring and reading, while the zeroing kills the systematic offset that repeats cannot touch.
medium.analogy: A checkout scale: the cashier tares the scales with the container first — the tare is the zeroing, the filled reading is the sale.
medium.examPointer: Write the subtraction sentence — mass of liquid equals mass of cylinder with liquid minus mass of cylinder — and attribute each error fix to its family.

check.stem: How is the liquid's mass obtained?

options.text: subtract the empty cylinder's mass from the filled cylinder's reading
options.explanation: The difference isolates the liquid.

options.text: read it directly from the cylinder's scale
options.explanation: The scale reads volume, not mass.

options.text: weigh the liquid in an open beaker only
options.explanation: The method weighs the cylinder, empty and filled.

options.text: multiply the volume by the density
options.explanation: That would need the density already known.

check.stem: Why is the balance zeroed with the empty cylinder on it?

options.text: to remove the systematic offset the cylinder's own mass would add
options.explanation: Zeroing kills the constant bias; repeats cannot.

options.text: to reduce the random error of pouring
options.explanation: Random error is the repeats' job.

options.text: because the balance cannot read a cylinder
options.explanation: The balance reads anything placed on it.

options.text: to warm the balance up
options.explanation: Warm-up is not the cited reason.

check.stem: Which hazard belongs in this practical's safety notes alongside its glassware?

options.text: pouring water onto the electric balance risks a shock
options.explanation: The safety notes warn exactly this.

options.text: the eureka can's steam burns
options.explanation: No steam appears in a density practical.

options.text: radioactive samples under test
options.explanation: Nothing radioactive is involved.

options.text: pressure vessels bursting
options.explanation: No pressurised equipment is used.

check.stem: Which error family do repeat-and-average fixes address?

options.text: random error
options.explanation: Averaging evens out scatter in both directions.

options.text: systematic error
options.explanation: Systematic offsets need re-zeroing or recalibration.

options.text: human dishonesty
options.explanation: The fix is statistical, not moral.

options.text: equipment failure
options.explanation: Broken equipment needs replacing, not averaging.

check.stem: A student records 50 g for the empty cylinder and 130 g with liquid aboard. The liquid's mass is

options.explanation: 130 − 50 = 80 grams of liquid.
That includes the cylinder.
That is the cylinder alone.
That adds instead of subtracting.

check.stem: State the mass-difference sentence used in the liquid experiment.
check.modelAnswer: Mass of liquid equals the mass of the cylinder with liquid minus the mass of the empty cylinder.

check.stem: State one systematic-error fix and one random-error fix from these experiments.
check.modelAnswer: Zeroing the digital balance before readings fixes a systematic error; repeating measurements and taking averages fixes random error.

check.stem: Explain why the measuring cylinder must never sit on the balance while water is poured into it.
check.modelAnswer: The balance is an electrical instrument and spilled water inside it can cause an electric shock, so the cylinder is filled away from the balance and only then placed aboard for the reading.

check.stem: A student obtains liquid masses of 78 g, 82 g and 80 g across three repeats. State the averaged mass and the density if the poured volume was 100 cm³.
check.modelAnswer: The averaged mass is (78 + 82 + 80) ÷ 3 = 80 g, and the density is 80 ÷ 100 = 0.8 g/cm³.

glossary.definition: A displacement can with a spout, used to collect the water displaced by a submerged object.
The pushing-out of water by a submerged object, whose volume equals the object's own volume.
The smallest change an instrument can reliably show, such as 0.01 g on the digital balance.
A constant offset in readings that repeats cannot remove, fixed by zeroing or recalibration.
Scatter in readings in either direction, reduced by repeating measurements and averaging.
